readings.title: The Shrine
readings.challenge: Track how one word of judgment, “useless,” is asked, borrowed and finally overruled.
readings.focus: Devotion to a place that offers no shelter, and value measured against use.
readings.context: The subtitle names a female presence who “watches over the sea”; the “you” addressed is both a rocky headland and the spirit of it. Galleys are oared ships; freesia is a fragrant flower. Read the four numbered sections as stages of one approach, from questioning the shore to hailing it.

excerpt.locator: Sea Garden, “The Shrine,” the whole poem, sections I–IV; opens “("SHE WATCHES OVER THE SEA")”; closes “…a little and the waves can never thrust us back from the splendour of your ragged coast.”.

questions.prompt: The first section opens with questions about harbours and trading ships. What standard of value do those questions assume, and how does “Nay” answer them?
facilitatorNotes: The questions measure the shore by its use to commerce: a graded crescent, a port, ships tempted out to trade. “Nay” answers by that same standard and finds the shore fierce, a “land-blight” that wrecks ships. The poem begins by condemning the place on practical terms.

questions.prompt: Who calls the shore “useless” in section II, and how does “I have heard” change the authority of the word?
facilitatorNotes: The landsmen say it; the speaker reports it as hearsay and sets “O grave, O beautiful” beside it, while “we” bring freesia to the shelf. The word becomes the verdict of people who value only shelter. Some readers hear the speaker half-agreeing, since the word is repeated twice; the offerings suggest the speakers value something the verdict cannot measure.
evidence: the landsmen tell it--I have heard--
we thread throat on throat of freesia

questions.prompt: Section III describes terror as flame and sparks rather than water. Is this shipwreck, a religious experience, or both?
facilitatorNotes: The speakers have gone further than the fisher-folk and are struck by a “bright shaft.” Fire and light suggest a divine encounter as much as a wreck, and the warnings of practical men return at the end of the section. Either reading should account for both the splendour and the “rifts” in it.

questions.prompt: The last section admits every danger the poem has listed. How can it still end in praise?
facilitatorNotes: Its “though” clauses concede splitting beams and floundering men, but the spirit has pardoned and touched the speakers, and the waves “can never thrust us back.” The commitment is now irreversible. Readers may find the ending ecstatic, fatal, or both, since the coast stays “ragged.”
evidence: your eyes have pardoned our faults,
from the splendour of your ragged coast.

readings.title: The Contest
readings.challenge: Sort the comparisons by material, stone, metal, tree and flower, and ask what each does to the body it describes.
readings.focus: A victor’s body praised as sculpture and landscape.
readings.context: The title recalls the athletic contests of ancient Greece, whose victors were crowned with wreaths, but the poem never shows a contest. It is a blazon, a catalogue praising parts of a body one comparison at a time. Torse is torso; citron and cistus (rock-rose) are Mediterranean plants.

excerpt.locator: Sea Garden, “The Contest,” the whole poem, sections I–III; opens “Your stature is modelled with straight tool-edge: you are chiselled like rocks that are…”; closes “…curved throat. Your shoulders are level-- they have melted rare silver for their breadth.”.

questions.prompt: Which words in section I come from carving or metalwork, and what do they suggest about how the speaker looks at this man?
facilitatorNotes: “Modelled,” “chiselled,” “tool-edge” and “worn brass” make him a finished artwork, hard and shaped. The rocks “eaten into by the sea” add erosion, as if strength has been carved by struggle. Readers may debate whether sculpture language admires him or keeps him at a distance.
evidence: there is a glint like worn brass.

questions.prompt: In section II he is first granite and ore, then “a limb of cypress / bent under a weight of snow.” What does the second comparison add?
facilitatorNotes: The rigid, mighty figure now bends under a load, so strength includes strain. The section then moves into motion: arms of fire, a sea treading on hill-slopes. The poem does not let him stay a statue.
evidence: bent under a weight of snow.

questions.prompt: Section III turns to plants. Do the flowers soften the figure, or does the poem keep its hardness?
facilitatorNotes: The narcissus “has copied” his breast, so nature imitates him rather than the reverse; his knees are “cut” from white-ash, and the last image returns to melted silver. Some readers find the flowers make him delicate; others see delicacy and strength fused. Either case needs the final metal image.
evidence: The narcissus has copied the arch

questions.prompt: The title promises a contest, but none happens. Where, if anywhere, is the contest?
facilitatorNotes: Possibilities: the band of gold and the myrtle suggest he is already the victor; the poem competes with sculpture to render a body; or the materials compete to describe him. A good answer explains why the poem withholds the event and keeps only the winner.
evidence: a great band clasps your forehead

readings.title: Sea Lily
readings.challenge: Follow the poem’s single turn and test whether damage and richness are really opposed.
readings.focus: A flower that is honoured by the forces that wound it.
readings.context: One of the book’s sea-flower poems, with “Sea Rose,” “Sea Poppies,” “Sea Violet” and “Sea Iris.” The lily is addressed as a “reed”; temple-steps recall the flowers left as offerings in ancient worship. Read it aloud twice, slowing at each dash.

excerpt.locator: Sea Garden, “Sea Lily,” the whole poem; opens “Reed, slashed and torn but doubly rich-- such great heads as yours drift upon…”; closes “…wind slash at your bark, you are lifted up, aye--though it hiss to cover you with froth.”.

questions.prompt: What does “but doubly rich” claim about a reed that is “slashed and torn”?
facilitatorNotes: The “but” sets richness against damage, yet “doubly” suggests the damage adds to the plant’s worth, or that it is rich both in its great heads and in surviving. Ask readers to choose a meaning and defend it from the rest of the poem.
evidence: slashed and torn but doubly rich--

questions.prompt: Heads like this one “drift upon temple-steps.” How does that comparison change being “shattered in the wind”?
facilitatorNotes: Flowers on temple steps are offerings, so scattering resembles worship rather than mere ruin. The wind becomes a kind of ritual hand. Some readers may still feel the plain loss in “shattered.”
evidence: you are shattered in the wind.

questions.prompt: Sand cuts the petal “like flint / on a bright stone.” What does the simile make of the damage?
facilitatorNotes: Flint strikes sparks and carves; a hard edge on a bright stone polishes or engraves it. The wound becomes a mark that makes brightness visible.
evidence: like flint on a bright stone.

questions.prompt: In the last stanza, is the lily lifted by the wind or rising against it?
facilitatorNotes: “You are lifted up” is passive, so the wind may be doing the lifting; but “Yet though” presents it as resistance, and “aye” concedes the hissing froth without retreat. The ambiguity is part of the poem’s point that force and endurance are hard to separate.

readings.title: The Wind Sleepers
readings.challenge: Identify the speakers from what they say and demand, since the poem never names them.
readings.focus: Spirits who require worship, and a poem that reads as ritual instructions.
readings.context: The “we” of the title once slept in the wind and have now woken. To propitiate is to win over a dangerous power with offerings; meted means measured out. Notice how the commands change from labour to song.

excerpt.locator: Sea Garden, “The Wind Sleepers,” the whole poem; opens “Whiter than the crust left by the tide, we are stung by the hurled sand and the broken…”; closes “…breaks into it, pour meted words of sea-hawks and gulls and sea-birds that cry discords.”.

questions.prompt: What do the speakers’ first descriptions of themselves suggest about what they are?
facilitatorNotes: They are whiter than the tide’s crust, stung by sand and shells, and they have fled “through the city gate.” They seem nature spirits once at rest in the wind, now restless and entering human space. Readers may also hear them as gods who have been neglected.
evidence: than the crust left by the tide,
we awoke and fled through the city gate.

questions.prompt: How do the commands change from “Tear-- / tear us an altar” to the end of the poem?
facilitatorNotes: Rough physical work on cliff-boulders gives way to a chant that never halts, then to “meted words.” The offering moves from building to singing to measured speech.

questions.prompt: Why should the offering be measured words of birds that “cry / discords”?
facilitatorNotes: Measure and discord pull against each other: the worship must be ordered yet keep the harsh sound of gulls and sea-hawks. Some readers take this as a description of H.D.’s own clipped, harsh style; the poem, short and unrhymed, may itself be such an offering.

readings.title: Evening
readings.challenge: Read two parallel stanzas that each end in loss, and compare what is lost in each.
readings.focus: Nightfall shown as a process: first light leaves, then shadow arrives.
readings.context: The edition prints “hypaticas” for hepaticas, early spring woodland flowers often blue; cornel is dogwood. Read the stanzas side by side and mark each verb of movement.

excerpt.locator: Sea Garden, “Evening,” the whole poem; opens “The light passes from ridge to ridge, from flower to flower-- the hypaticas, wide-spread…”; closes “…another leaf on the grass, shadow seeks shadow, then both leaf and leaf-shadow are lost.”.

questions.prompt: In the first stanza, how do the flowers take part in their own disappearance?
facilitatorNotes: As light passes, “the petals reach inward” and the tips bend toward the heart: the flowers close, so disappearing looks like an action, not only an absence of light.

questions.prompt: How does H.D. make the darkness in the second stanza seem alive?
facilitatorNotes: Shadows “dart,” black “creeps,” a leaf “cuts” another leaf, and shadow “seeks” shadow. The verbs belong to animals and searchers, so the dark has intention.

questions.prompt: Both stanzas end with “lost.” Is the ending sad, calm, or neither?
facilitatorNotes: The repeated word can sound like an elegy, but the description stays exact and unemotional. The final image, a leaf and its shadow lost together, joins a thing and its image at the moment both vanish. Readers may hear peace, loss, or simple accuracy; ask for the words that decide it.

readings.title: Sea Poppies
readings.challenge: Explain why a poem about a flower gives most of its lines to a husk and to the ground it grows in.
readings.focus: The language of wealth applied to beach debris and a hardy plant.
readings.context: A husk is a dry outer casing; conch-shells are large spiral sea shells. The yellow horned poppy grows on shingle beaches. As in “Sea Rose,” a shore plant is compared with flowers of richer ground.

excerpt.locator: Sea Garden, “Sea Poppies,” the whole poem; opens “Amber husk fluted with gold, fruit on the sand marked with a rich grain,”; closes “…wide-spread, fire upon leaf, what meadow yields so fragrant a leaf as your bright leaf?”.

questions.prompt: Which words in the first two stanzas come from the language of wealth, and what do they make of the husk?
facilitatorNotes: Amber, gold, rich grain and treasure price a seed-case like jewellery. “Spilled” and “to bleach” suggest that this wealth is scattered and wasted, valued by no one but the speaker.

questions.prompt: Why list the debris among which the stalk “has caught root”?
facilitatorNotes: Wet pebbles, drift and grated or split shells are broken, infertile matter. Rooting there shows tenacity, and “caught” suggests both chance and grip.

questions.prompt: The poem ends with a question. What answer does it expect, and has the poem earned it?
facilitatorNotes: It expects “none”: no meadow yields so fragrant a leaf. “Fire upon leaf” gives the flower its colour, but the earlier stanzas offered sight and texture, not scent, so some readers will say the claim arrives unprepared; others that the treasure language has prepared for an extravagant verdict.

readings.title: Loss
readings.challenge: Account for a speaker who says “I am glad” about a death.
readings.focus: A battlefield elegy that becomes a portrait of the dead.
readings.context: The speaker is one of a few soldiers trapped between a marsh and a cliff in an unnamed ancient battle; as in “Prisoners,” no historical event is identified. Greaves are armour for the shins; the estuary is where the river meets the sea.
readings.contentNote: Soldiers are killed in battle, one wounded in the side; the speaker grieves a drowned companion.

excerpt.locator: Sea Garden, “Loss,” the whole poem; opens “The sea called-- you faced the estuary, you were drowned as the tide passed.-- I am glad…”; closes “…how I crowded before the spearsmen-- but the gods wanted you, the gods wanted you back.”.

questions.prompt: Why is the speaker “glad” that the beloved drowned?
facilitatorNotes: Drowning is an escape from the stifling mist, the “curious torture,” and the enemy’s lances; the others die in pain. The gladness is grief arguing with itself. Some readers hear bitterness or shock in it.

questions.prompt: How does the poem tell the other deaths, and why so briefly?
facilitatorNotes: One pierced man drags himself across the marsh; another crawls too late; a single stanza sums up all three fates. The brevity contrasts with the long description of the beloved: grief is selective, and attention shows love.
evidence: the four of us--somehow shut off.
and the tide swept you out.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker admire in the beloved, and why does the poem dwell on it after a battle?
facilitatorNotes: Strength joined to beauty: slight yet almost as tall as the lance-bearers, a strong wrist, shorn locks, a sunburnt neck, a body “no garment could deface.” The memory insists on the living body against its loss.
evidence: but never beauty welded with strength.

questions.prompt: The last stanza confesses, “I wonder if you knew how I watched.” How does this change your reading of the opening gladness?
facilitatorNotes: It reveals an unspoken love, so the earlier relief may be a way of bearing loss. “The gods wanted you back” consoles by making the beloved almost divine, though the repetition can sound resigned or resentful.
evidence: I wonder if you knew how I watched,

readings.title: Huntress
readings.challenge: Hear how the poem’s rhythm imitates the pace it describes.
readings.focus: An invitation that is also a challenge; speed and heat valued over the catch.
readings.context: The title recalls Artemis, the Greek goddess of the hunt, and her companions, but the poem names no one. A group of hunters speaks to someone lagging behind; the italic lines are their call.

excerpt.locator: Sea Garden, “Huntress,” the whole poem; opens “Come, blunt your spear with us, our pace is hot and our bare heels in the heel-prints--…”; closes “…follow the quickest one, aye, though you leave the trail and drop exhausted at our feet.”.

questions.prompt: Is “Come, blunt your spear with us” an invitation or a taunt?
facilitatorNotes: Both: it welcomes the listener into the hunt, then asks whether they are “already beaten.” To blunt a spear is to use it hard, perhaps until it is worn. The questions test the listener before admitting them.
evidence: Come, blunt your spear with us,

questions.prompt: How do the details of the third stanza complicate the picture of a hunt?
facilitatorNotes: The hunters cross ploughed land, drag the seed from the clefts and break clods with their heels before whirling into the woods. Wildness runs over farming and damages it; some readers see a contrast between cultivated order and the hunt’s freedom.
evidence: dragged the seed from the clefts,

questions.prompt: The poem ends with the listener dropping “exhausted at our feet.” What does it value more than success?
facilitatorNotes: No prey ever appears. The command is to follow the quickest even off the trail, so intensity and effort count more than the catch; collapse at the hunters’ feet still counts as joining them.
evidence: and drop exhausted at our feet.

readings.title: Sea Violet
readings.challenge: Follow a comparison among violets and find the speaker’s preference.
readings.focus: Choosing the frail, exposed flower over the showier one.
readings.context: Agate is a banded semi-precious stone. In “Sea Gods” violets were brought by the armful as offerings; here a single violet stands on the edge of a sand-hill.

excerpt.locator: Sea Garden, “Sea Violet,” the whole poem; opens “The white violet is scented on its stalk, the sea-violet fragile as agate, lies fronting…”; closes “…the edge of the sand-hill, but you catch the light-- frost, a star edges with its fire.”.

questions.prompt: Is the white violet of the first lines the same flower as the sea-violet? What evidence supports each reading?
facilitatorNotes: The lines could name two flowers, one scented on its stalk and one fragile on the sand-bank; but the second stanza’s “white sort” set against the blue hill violets suggests the sea-violet is the white one. Let readers argue either way from the punctuation and from the second stanza.
evidence: one root of the white sort?

questions.prompt: Why repeat “who would change for these”?
facilitatorNotes: The repetition insists: the speaker refuses to trade even one root of the white violet for the greater blue violets fluttering on the hill. The question expects the answer “no one,” but the doubling also sounds like an argument still being won.
evidence: who would change for these who would change for these

questions.prompt: How does the final line turn a frail grasp into something powerful?
facilitatorNotes: The violet “catch[es] the light” like frost, and a star “edges” it with fire. Cold and fire combine, and a tiny flower is compared with a star; the syntax is compressed, so readers may parse it in more than one way.
evidence: frost, a star edges with its fire.

readings.title: The Cliff Temple
readings.challenge: Track the shift from describing a place to pursuing a god who keeps withdrawing.
readings.focus: Worship as a frustrated pursuit, with the sacred always further off.
readings.context: Greek temples were often built on headlands above the sea; this god is never named. The first section describes the temple and its height, and the next three follow a speaker who has climbed to it.
readings.contentNote: In section III the speaker asks whether to leap from the cliff.

excerpt.locator: Sea Garden, “The Cliff Temple,” the whole poem, sections I–IV; opens “Great, bright portal, shelf of rock, rocks fitted in long ledges, rocks fitted to dark,…”; closes “…on your portal and I know-- you are further than this, still further on another cliff.”.

questions.prompt: In section I, what makes the temple “the world-edge”?
facilitatorNotes: Its height and isolation: no goat or mountain-sheep has stepped on its grass, sea-hawks shout overhead, and the breakers below are silent. It is set apart from ordinary life and almost touches the sky.
evidence: you lift, you are the world-edge,

questions.prompt: How does the small tree in section I prepare for the speaker of the later sections?
facilitatorNotes: It stiffens and bends in the gale, yet its flowers are fragrant at that height: endurance at the edge. The speaker is also “splintered and torn” by the climb. Some readers see a parallel; others a contrast, since the tree holds its place while the speaker lurches and stumbles.
evidence: a small tree stiffens in the gale,

questions.prompt: The speaker both adores and accuses the god. Find each and explain how they can coexist.
facilitatorNotes: “Dear--mysterious--beautiful” sits beside a call for a daemon to taunt the god with “his evil and his vice.” Love that cannot reach its object turns to anger at the one who withdraws; the poem keeps both feelings rather than resolving them.
evidence: taunt him with his evil and his vice.

questions.prompt: What does section IV conclude about the search?
facilitatorNotes: The temple is not the god’s final dwelling: he is “further than this, / still further on another cliff.” The ending can be read as despair or as a renewed call to climb; the speaker now “know[s]” something the climb has taught.

readings.title: Sea Iris
readings.challenge: Notice how the questions of the second section replace the direct praise of the first.
readings.focus: A brittle flower praised through scent, colour and an imagined history of its colour.
readings.context: The last of the book’s sea-flower poems. Ancient dyers took a costly purple from the murex, a sea snail, so murex-fishers gathered them along the shore. Myrrh and camphor are strong-scented resins.

excerpt.locator: Sea Garden, “Sea Iris,” the whole poem, sections I–II; opens “Weed, moss-weed, root tangled in sand, sea-iris, brittle flower, one petal like a shell…”; closes “…the waves, you are painted blue, painted like a fresh prow stained among the salt weeds.”.

questions.prompt: The first section combines damage with praise. Which words show both, and how does “Fortunate one” fit?
facilitatorNotes: The flower is brittle and one petal is broken, yet it is “scented and stinging,” wind in the nostrils. Its fortune lies in intensity rather than wholeness.
evidence: one petal like a shell is broken,

questions.prompt: Why does the second section ask questions about murex-fishers and gold?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker imagines where the colour came from: dye splashed by fishers, roots drawing colour from the sand, gold riveted underneath. Human crafts are offered to explain a natural colour, and leaving the questions unanswered keeps the wonder open.
evidence: Do the murex-fishers drench you as they pass?

questions.prompt: How does the closing simile connect the flower to the sea and to human making?
facilitatorNotes: The iris is “painted like a fresh prow,” the bow of a boat newly painted blue above the waves, yet “stained” among salt weeds. Craft and nature meet, and freshness already shows wear.
